# Pings: label, never drop, and the ping rate {#sec-pings}

::: {.callout-note}
**Drafted by AI, in part.** "The tests, in order" was written by Claude (Anthropic) on 2026-10-20, on ramb's example
data. The other sections are still a skeleton, outlined from the maintainer's direction (plan 033 §4) and the reading
map of the groups' reports (`ices_reports.yml`). Reviewed by: nobody yet.
:::

```{r setup}
#| include: false
# quarto's R may start in a C locale; keep characters such as the degree sign intact
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))
library(tidyverse)
library(ramb)
library(patchwork)

# the Danish tracks (WKSSFGEO), in the grammar's column names, a ping every ten seconds
dansk <- rb_read_example("dansk") |> collect() |>
  rename(vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp) |>
  arrange(vid, time)
harbours <- rb_read_example("dansk_harbours") |> collect()
harbours <- sf::st_sf(port_id = harbours$SI_HARB,
                      geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(structure(harbours$geometry, class = "WKB"), crs = 4326))

# implied speed of each ping against its predecessor, in knots
implied_kn <- function(d) {
  d |> arrange(time) |>
    mutate(dt = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "secs")),
           kn = rb_calc_distance(lag(lon), lag(lat), lon, lat) / dt * 1.94384)
}
flag_colours <- c(kept = "grey70", forward = "#C0504D", vmask = "#E69F00", duplicate = "#4F81BD",
                  invalid = "black")
log_kn <- scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = c("0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1000"))
theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

**In the diagram:** the second row, *Flag pings* (`flag_pings`). Its tests run in order, each on pings not yet flagged:
invalid (placeholder) → duplicate (second feed) → impossible (set aside) → port (kept in the trail). The band below
it says that **the ping rate sets how far down a track can go**: interpolate or downsample to a regular series, and
keep the gaps and the device.

## The problem

- Raw positions hold placeholders (0, 0), copies from a second feed, and jumps no vessel can make.
- Dropping them loses the record of what was wrong. Labelling them keeps it, so pings in equal pings out.
- How often a vessel reports decides everything below it. A ping every hour cannot show a 20-minute haul.

## What the groups say

- Cleaning steps: time checks, duplicates, outliers, points in harbours and boat parking areas (WKSSFGEO 2022,
  pp. 18-19).
- A longitude sign error, and before-and-after cleaning summaries (WGSFD 2015, pp. 12, 24).
- Overlapping national and NEAFC feeds (WGSFD 2015, pp. 12-13); feeds merged with a spline (WKSSFGEO 2022, p. 9).
- Polling rates: higher or variable VMS rates (WGSFD 2016, p. 60), iVMS (WGSFD 2016, p. 31), what member states poll
  (WGSFD 2025a, p. 3), a recommended minimum for small vessels (WGSFD 2025b, p. 14), and what counts as
  high-resolution data (WGSFD 2025b, p. 23).
- Low-cost tracking (WKSSFGEO2 2023, p. 1); mooring sites found from the track (WKSSFGEO2 2023, p. 6).

## From ramb's articles

- *trips* ("Step 0: flag the pings"): the four flaggers on `dansk`, with `dansk_harbours` for ports.
- *trips* ("Trouble pings that bend the track"): vessel `EX_10` on 6 October 2013, sixteen impossible positions that
  drag the line, before and after.
- *trips* ("Side point: when the flagged pings sit on the track"): a dense and a sparse feed of `EX_10` interleaved.
  Speed against the last kept ping flags innocent dense pings, and flagging duplicates first repairs it.
- *tools* ("Track calculations", "Interpolation"): distances, speeds and step times; `rb_interpolate_track()`
  putting positions onto event times.

## The tests, in order

Every test in this row adds a label to the ping and removes nothing. The labels are applied in order, and each test
looks only at pings the earlier ones have left unflagged. At the end, the flagged pings sit in their own table and
the rest go on to the trip. Pings in equal pings out, and every one of them can still be inspected.

### Invalid: placeholders

A placeholder is a position that was never a fix: a receiver that has not found its satellites, or a database that
fills an empty field with zeros. The most famous is (0, 0), a spot in the Gulf of Guinea that geographers call Null
Island. In raw tracking data it can look like the busiest fishing ground on Earth. `rb_flag_ping_invalid()` catches
two kinds. The first is a longitude equal to its latitude, which (0, 0) is. The second is a position outside the
globe.

ramb's example sets are clean in this respect: not one of their pings is a placeholder. So the case below plants
three in a real day of a Danish vessel, at the times a receiver might lose its fix (@fig-invalid, @tbl-invalid).

```{r}
#| label: fig-invalid
#| fig-cap: "One day of a Danish vessel (`dansk`, EX_3, 18 September 2020), with three planted placeholders. Left: the track as it would be drawn with them, by way of Null Island. Right: the same day once they are labelled `invalid` and set aside."
#| fig-height: 3.6
day <- dansk |> filter(vid == "EX_3", as_date(time) == as.Date("2020-09-18")) |>
  select(vid, time, lon, lat, speed)
planted <- day |> slice(c(800, 1900, 3000)) |>
  mutate(lon = c(0, 0, 181), lat = c(0, 0, 57), time = time + 1)
day_raw <- bind_rows(day, planted) |> arrange(time) |> rb_flag_ping_invalid()
world <- map_data("world")
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = "grey90") +
  geom_path(data = day_raw |> filter(abs(lon) <= 180), aes(lon, lat), colour = "#C0504D", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 4, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = -4, label = "Null Island", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-20, 25), ylim = c(-8, 62)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "as recorded")
p2 <- ggplot(day_raw |> filter(is.na(ping_flag)), aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "placeholders set aside")
p1 + p2
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-invalid
#| tbl-cap: "The planted pings and the label each one gets. The longitude of 181 is outside the globe; the two at (0, 0) have a longitude equal to their latitude."
day_raw |> filter(!is.na(ping_flag)) |>
  transmute(time = format(time, "%H:%M:%S"), lon, lat, ping_flag) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Duplicate: the second feed

A vessel can be heard by more than one system at once: two AIS receivers, AIS and VMS, a national feed and a
regional one. Each report arrives twice, seconds and metres apart, and the copy is not always a perfect copy. The
groups met this early on, with national and NEAFC data overlapping (WGSFD 2015, pp. 12-13), and the workshops merged
feeds into one series (WKSSFGEO 2022, p. 9).

The `dansk` data hold a clear case on one vessel, `EX_10`, on 19 July 2014. Most of the day is a dense stream: a
ping every ten seconds, steady and self-consistent. Mixed into it is a sparse stream, a ping a minute, always at 39 or
40 seconds past the minute, whose positions lie a little off the dense track. The data carry no column naming the
feed, so the feed is read from that cadence here. Real data would name it.

Order matters (@fig-duplicate). Run the speed test alone, and each sparse ping makes the next honest dense ping look
like a jump, so innocent pings are flagged. Flag the copies first, with the dense stream given priority, and the
speed test then finds only the one real spike.

```{r}
#| label: fig-duplicate
#| fig-cap: "Vessel EX_10 on 19 July 2014 (`dansk`): the implied speed of each ping against the one before it, coloured by its label, with the 25-knot ceiling dashed. Top: the speed test alone. Bottom: duplicates flagged first, with the dense feed given priority; every sparse ping is labelled `duplicate`, and only the true spike is flagged by speed."
#| fig-height: 5.5
two <- dansk |> filter(vid == "EX_10", as_date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-19")) |>
  select(vid, time, lon, lat) |>
  mutate(feed = if_else(second(time) %in% c(39, 40), "sparse", "dense"))
alone <- two |> rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean")
first <- two |> rb_flag_ping_duplicate(priority = c("dense", "sparse"), feed = feed, max_dt_s = 15) |>
  rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean")
show <- function(x, title) {
  x |> implied_kn() |> filter(!is.na(kn)) |>
    mutate(label = coalesce(ping_flag, "kept")) |>
    arrange(label != "kept") |>
    ggplot(aes(time, kn, colour = label)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.7, show.legend = TRUE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
    log_kn +
    scale_colour_manual(values = flag_colours, limits = c("kept", "duplicate", "forward", "vmask")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "implied speed (kn, log)", colour = NULL, title = title)
}
show(alone, "speed test alone") / show(first, "duplicates flagged first") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-duplicate
#| tbl-cap: "The same day: the labels each feed's pings get, with and without the duplicate test run first."
bind_rows(alone |> mutate(order = "speed test alone"),
          first |> mutate(order = "duplicates first")) |>
  count(order, feed, label = coalesce(ping_flag, "kept")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Impossible: set aside

A position the vessel cannot have reached, at the speed it would have needed, is flagged and set aside.
`rb_flag_ping_impossible()` measures each ping against the last one it kept, with a ceiling of 25 knots by default.
On the morning of 6 October 2013 the same vessel, `EX_10`, was halfway through a three-day trip. Sixteen of its 34
pings that morning leap up to tens of kilometres off the grounds and back within minutes, while the speed it reported
stayed near six knots (@fig-impossible). A flagged ping can sit below the ceiling in the speed plot, and a kept one
above it: the test measures each ping against the last ping it kept, not against its raw neighbour, so the return to
the track after a spike is judged against the last good position.

```{r}
#| label: fig-impossible
#| fig-cap: "Vessel EX_10, 6 October 2013, 05:00 to 13:30 (`dansk`). Left: the track as recorded (grey) and once the impossible pings are set aside (blue), with those pings in red. Right: each ping's implied speed, log scale; the spikes sit far above the 25-knot ceiling."
#| fig-height: 4
morning <- dansk |>
  filter(vid == "EX_10", time >= as.POSIXct("2013-10-06 05:00", tz = "UTC"),
         time <= as.POSIXct("2013-10-06 13:30", tz = "UTC")) |>
  select(vid, time, lon, lat) |>
  rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean")
q1 <- ggplot(morning, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_path(data = morning |> filter(is.na(ping_flag)), colour = "#4F81BD", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = morning |> filter(!is.na(ping_flag)), colour = "#C0504D", size = 1.5) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
q2 <- morning |> implied_kn() |> filter(!is.na(kn)) |>
  mutate(label = coalesce(ping_flag, "kept")) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, kn, colour = label)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  log_kn +
  scale_colour_manual(values = flag_colours) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "implied speed (kn, log)", colour = NULL)
q1 + q2
```

How well does the test do when the answer is known? `whacks1` is a short track made up for the purpose: 46 pings, 12
of them deliberately misplaced. The five methods of `rb_flag_ping_impossible()` differ in how much of the
surrounding track they consult (@tbl-whacks). On this track, the forward and sequential methods flag exactly the
twelve. The default, `"clean"`, and `"sda"` also catch all twelve, but take four good pings with them. `"fwdbwd"`
finds two. One small made-up track does not decide between methods; the comparison over real labelled tracks is
@sec-validation's.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-whacks
#| tbl-cap: "The five methods on `whacks1`, a made-up track of 46 pings with 12 known misplacements."
w <- rb_read_example("whacks1") |> collect() |> mutate(vid = as.character(vid))
map_dfr(c("clean", "sda", "forward", "fwdbwd", "sequential"), function(m) {
  f <- rb_flag_ping_impossible(w, method = m)
  tibble(method = m, flagged = sum(!is.na(f$ping_flag)),
         `misplaced, caught` = sum(!is.na(f$ping_flag) & f$whacks),
         `good, flagged` = sum(!is.na(f$ping_flag) & !f$whacks))
}) |> knitr::kable()
```

Across the whole of `dansk`, 395,558 pings, the default test flags `r format(sum(!is.na(rb_flag_ping_impossible(dansk, method = "clean")$ping_flag)), big.mark = ",")`:
about one in two thousand. Few, but each one bends a line on a map.

### Port: kept in the trail

A ping inside a harbour polygon is not wrong. It is a vessel in port, and the next row needs it, because trips are cut
on port calls. `rb_flag_ping_port()` gives such a ping the port's id and keeps it in the trail. The groups have
argued both ways here: harbour and steaming pings left in the aggregates (WGSFD 2014, p. 7), points in harbours and in
boat parking areas (WKSSFGEO 2022, p. 19), and mooring sites found from the track where no list exists (WKSSFGEO2
2023, p. 6).

In `dansk`, about one ping in six is in port (@fig-port). A vessel at the quay with its transmitter on reports a ping
every ten seconds all night, which is why the share is so high, and three of the fourteen vessels spend most of their
pings tied up. Dropping port pings would hide that, and the trip row would lose the port calls it is cut on.

```{r}
#| label: fig-port
#| fig-cap: "Pings in port (`dansk`, with `dansk_harbours`). Left: the busiest harbour of the data, its polygon and the pings inside it. Right: the share of each vessel's pings in port."
#| fig-height: 4
clean <- dansk |> select(vid, time, lon, lat) |>
  rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean") |> filter(is.na(ping_flag)) |>
  rb_flag_ping_port(harbours)
top <- clean |> filter(!is.na(port_id)) |> count(port_id, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1) |> pull(port_id)
poly <- harbours |> filter(port_id == top)
bb <- sf::st_bbox(poly)
near <- clean |> filter(between(lon, bb["xmin"] - 0.01, bb["xmax"] + 0.01),
                        between(lat, bb["ymin"] - 0.005, bb["ymax"] + 0.005))
r1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = poly, fill = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.3, colour = "#E69F00") +
  geom_point(data = near, aes(lon, lat, colour = !is.na(port_id)), size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#C0504D", `FALSE` = "grey60"), labels = c("at sea", "in port"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
r2 <- clean |> group_by(vid) |> summarise(in_port = mean(!is.na(port_id))) |>
  ggplot(aes(in_port, reorder(vid, in_port))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#E69F00") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "pings in port", y = NULL)
r1 + r2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1))
```

### The band: the ping rate

How often a vessel reports decides how far down the diagram its track can go. Every member state polls its VMS at its
own rate (WGSFD 2025a, p. 3). The group now recommends about a ping every 30 seconds for small vessels (WGSFD 2025b,
p. 14), and takes "high resolution" to mean a ping every ten minutes or less (WGSFD 2025b, p. 23).

ramb's example sets span most of that range (@fig-intervals): from ten seconds in the Danish data and thirty in the
Portuguese GPS loggers, to ten minutes in the Irish inshore VMS and the survey tracks. None of them is as sparse as
the hourly or two-hourly VMS that much of the ICES data call still rests on. That case has to be made by thinning a
dense track.

```{r}
#| label: fig-intervals
#| fig-cap: "The interval between consecutive pings in each of ramb's example sets, log scale. The dashed lines mark one and two hours, the polling of classic VMS."
#| fig-height: 4.5
std <- function(s) {
  x <- rb_read_example(s) |> collect()
  x <- switch(s,
    dansk = rename(x, vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp),
    wkssfgeo_adriatic_passive = rename(x, vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp),
    wkssfgeo_cnr_ais = rename(x, vid = MMSI, time = datetime),
    creel = rename(x, vid = id),
    x)
  x |> transmute(set = s, vid = as.character(vid), time)
}
sets <- c("dansk", "wkssfgeo_pt_gps", "wkssfgeo2_pt_gps", "creel", "ird_mg_gillnet", "wkssfgeo2_it_pots",
          "wkssfgeo_adriatic_passive", "wkssfgeo_cnr_ais", "wkssfgeo2_irl_pots", "wkssfgeo2_irl_gillnets", "trawlsurvey")
intervals <- map_dfr(sets, std) |>
  arrange(set, vid, time) |>
  group_by(set, vid) |>
  mutate(minutes = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "mins"))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(minutes > 0)
ggplot(intervals, aes(minutes, reorder(set, minutes, median))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.2, outlier.alpha = 0.2, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(60, 120), linetype = 2, colour = "#C0504D") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 60, 1440), labels = c("6 s", "1 min", "10 min", "1 h", "1 day")) +
  labs(x = "interval between pings", y = NULL)
```

Thinning shows what a lower rate costs. One day of a Danish vessel, recorded every ten seconds, is cut down to one ping
a minute, every ten minutes, every hour and every two hours (@fig-thin). At ten minutes the day's shape is still
there. At an hour it is a sketch. At two hours it is a few straight lines across the ground the vessel worked.

```{r}
#| label: fig-thin
#| fig-cap: "One day of vessel EX_3 (`dansk`, 18 September 2020), at its own ten-second rate and thinned to one ping a minute, every ten minutes, every hour and every two hours."
#| fig-height: 2.3
thin <- function(x, mins) x |> mutate(b = as.numeric(time) %/% (mins * 60)) |>
  distinct(vid, b, .keep_all = TRUE) |> select(-b)
rates <- c(`10 s` = 0, `1 min` = 1, `10 min` = 10, `1 h` = 60, `2 h` = 120)
thinned <- imap_dfr(rates, function(m, nm) (if (m == 0) day else thin(day, m)) |> mutate(rate = nm)) |>
  mutate(rate = factor(rate, names(rates)))
ggplot(thinned, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = thinned |> filter(rate %in% c("1 h", "2 h", "10 min")), size = 0.6, colour = "#C0504D") +
  facet_wrap(~ rate, nrow = 1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Interpolation puts positions back between the pings that remain. The question is how far off they land
(@fig-interp). Here each thinned track is interpolated in a straight line back to the original ten-second times, with
`rb_interpolate_track()`, and compared with where the vessel really was. A ping a minute misses by a metre or two. At
ten minutes the typical miss is about 20 metres, but one in ten is off by more than 250. At an hour the typical miss is
about 700 metres, and at two hours about two kilometres, with the worst several kilometres away. Straight lines know
nothing of a vessel's turns. An interpolation that uses the vessel's course and speed does better (a cubic Hermite
spline, which the workshops used), and is not yet in ramb.

```{r}
#| label: fig-interp
#| fig-cap: "How far a straight-line interpolation lands from the true position, for the same day thinned to each rate (log scale). Times before the first or after the last remaining ping cannot be interpolated and are left out."
#| fig-height: 3
miss <- imap_dfr(rates[-1], function(m, nm) {
  ip <- rb_interpolate_track(day |> select(vid, time), thin(day, m) |> select(vid, time, lon, lat), by = "vid")
  tibble(rate = nm, metres = rb_calc_distance(day$lon, day$lat, ip$lon, ip$lat))
}) |>
  filter(!is.na(metres)) |>
  mutate(rate = factor(rate, names(rates)[-1]))
ggplot(miss, aes(metres, rate)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3, outlier.alpha = 0.3, fill = "grey90") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(), breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000)) +
  labs(x = "distance from the true position (m, log)", y = "thinned to")
```

## Methods compared

- Flagging impossible pings by a speed threshold against the cleaning in ramb (`rb_flag_ping_impossible`,
  method "clean"). Graphic: what each removes on `whacks1`.

## What if a source is missing

- No port list: ports unknown, so port pings stay unlabelled. Show the effect on the trips of the next chapter.
- A sparse feed only (hourly VMS): which flags still work, and which pings can no longer be judged.

## Checking it

- Pings in equal pings out across the trail and the set-aside table: a bar per dataset.

## In the ICES data call

- The data call drops the pings it does not keep. This book labels them instead, so totals can be traced back.

## With ramb

- `rb_flag_ping_invalid()`, `rb_flag_ping_duplicate()`, `rb_flag_ping_impossible()`, `rb_flag_ping_port()`,
  `rb_detect_in_polygons()`, `rb_calc_speed()`, `rb_calc_speed_smooth()`, `rb_calc_step_time()`,
  `rb_interpolate_track()`, `rb_summarise_track()`.

## Not yet in ramb

- Interpolation that uses course and speed (cubic Hermite), and downsampling as a function.
